nodes.name: Murch's Rule of Six
nodes.summary: Every cut must be judged against six criteria in strict priority order. When criteria conflict, sacrifice from the bottom, never from the top. Emotion outweighs everything.

details.principle: Every cut must be judged against six criteria, in strict priority order. When criteria conflict, sacrifice from the bottom, never from the top. Emotion outweighs everything.
details.author: Walter Murch, 'In the Blink of an Eye' (2001)
details.application: The signal system primarily operates on criteria 3-6 (rhythm, eye-trace, planarity, spatial) because these are measurable. Criteria 1-2 (emotion, story) require understanding MEANING — provided by the Unified Intelligence Engine through creative intent and moment weighting. The moment_weight_map IS the emotion/story layer.
examples: A cut emotionally perfect that advances the story is forgiven for awkward eye-trace
A spatially perfect cut that's emotionally wrong cannot be saved
implications: Satisfying higher criteria obscures problems with lower criteria
Signal-based mechanical precision is subordinate to emotion and story
moment_weight_map is the emotion/story layer above mechanical signals

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 1: Emotion (51%)
nodes.summary: The dominant criterion. Does the cut feel right? What should the audience feel at this moment?

details.principle: EMOTION (51%) — Does the cut feel right? What should the audience feel at this moment?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: When the cut is emotionally perfect, the viewer forgives all lower-tier failures. This is the LLM/creative-intent layer.
implications: Emotion is the single most weighted criterion
Creative intent decisions trump mechanical signal decisions

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 2: Story (23%)
nodes.summary: Does the cut advance the narrative? Does it bring new information?

details.principle: STORY (23%) — Does the cut advance the narrative? Does it bring new information?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: Combined with emotion, accounts for 74% of cut judgment. Information must move forward across the cut.
implications: Cuts that don't advance narrative are suspect
New information per cut is the second-highest virtue

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 3: Rhythm (10%)
nodes.summary: Is the timing musically right? Does it feel natural in the sequence's flow?

details.principle: RHYTHM (10%) — Is the timing musically right? Does it feel natural in the sequence's flow?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: First measurable criterion — handled by Editron's signal system (pacing mappings, beat-sync).
implications: Rhythm is the gateway between meaning-driven and mechanical criteria
Signal system can compute this directly

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 4: Eye-Trace (7%)
nodes.summary: Does the viewer's eye land naturally on the important element in the next shot?

details.principle: EYE-TRACE (7%) — Does the viewer's eye land naturally on the important element in the next shot?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: Across-cut visual continuity for attention. Subject-position tracking and salience mapping inform this.
implications: Subject position from clip A should align with subject position in clip B
Visual saliency analysis can support this signal

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 5: Planarity (5%)
nodes.summary: Does the 2D screen composition read correctly?

details.principle: PLANARITY (5%) — Does the 2D screen composition read correctly?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: 2D screen composition continuity across cuts. Rule of thirds, balance, framing alignment.
implications: Composition jumps create visual discomfort even when content is right

nodes.name: Rule of Six — Priority 6: Spatial (4%)
nodes.summary: Does 3D space make sense across the cut?

details.principle: SPATIAL (4%) — Does 3D space make sense across the cut?
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: 180-degree rule, screen direction continuity, spatial geography of the scene.
implications: Lowest-priority criterion — sacrificed first when higher criteria conflict
Crossing the line is forgivable when emotion/story benefit

nodes.name: Murch's Blink Theory
nodes.summary: Cuts should land where the viewer would naturally blink — at cognitive/emotional transition points where the brain has completed processing and is ready for new input.

details.principle: Cuts should land where the viewer would naturally blink — at cognitive/emotional transition points. Blinks occur when the brain completes processing a thought and is ready for new input. A well-timed cut feels like blinking — invisible. A badly-timed cut feels like someone forced your eyes shut mid-thought.
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: Cuts at semantic/cognitive boundaries (end of phrase, post-action, post-emotional-beat) feel invisible; cuts mid-thought feel violent.
implications: Detect cognitive completion points as cut candidates
Topic boundaries and speech endings are blink candidates

nodes.name: Murch's Lingering Principle
nodes.summary: Cutting away before the speaker finishes makes the audience take words at face value. Lingering 1-2 seconds after speech ends invites the audience to study the face and read deeper meaning.

details.principle: Cutting away BEFORE the speaker finishes = audience takes words at face value. Lingering 1-2 seconds AFTER speech ends = audience studies the face, questions sincerity, reads deeper meaning. The same content with different cut timing creates different interpretations.
details.author: Walter Murch
details.application: Hold duration after speech ending is itself a creative decision — same words, different meanings depending on linger time.
implications: Post-speech hold length determines interpretation depth
The editor doesn't change what was said — they change how the viewer PROCESSES what was said
Useful for sincerity testing, dramatic irony, post-statement weight

nodes.name: Pearlman's Breath-Rhythm Model
nodes.summary: Editing rhythm follows the body's rhythm — we perceive time in breath cycles of inhale (tension/anticipation) and exhale (release/satisfaction).

details.principle: Editing rhythm is not mechanical — it follows the body's rhythm. We perceive time in breath cycles.
details.author: Karen Pearlman, 'Cutting Rhythms' (2009, 3rd ed. 2024)
details.application: Without Pearlman's model, the system would produce mechanically correct but physically exhausting output. The breath model is why the system needs to HOLD sometimes (inhale) and CUT sometimes (exhale), and why the pattern must vary.
implications: Pacing must alternate hold and release
organic_imperfection_injection and post_peak_decompression mappings implement breath
The pattern of inhale/exhale must vary, not metronomic

nodes.name: Inhale — Tension/Anticipation
nodes.summary: Holding a shot past comfortable creates an inhale — the viewer tenses, expects the cut. The moment before the cut is charged with anticipation.

details.principle: Inhale = tension/anticipation. Holding a shot past comfortable creates an inhale — the viewer tenses, expects the cut. The moment BEFORE the cut is charged with anticipation. Energy is building. The viewer's body is literally bracing.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: Deliberately holding past comfort point builds tension. Used before climactic cuts.
implications: Hold-past-expected creates physical tension in the viewer
Inhale phase is preparation for impact

nodes.name: Exhale — Release/Satisfaction
nodes.summary: Cutting provides release — the viewer exhales, energy dissipates. Early cuts create propulsion; late cuts amplify release.

details.principle: Exhale = release/satisfaction. Cutting provides release — the viewer exhales, energy dissipates. The new shot is fresh input. If the cut comes slightly EARLY (before the viewer fully expects it), it creates propulsion — the viewer is pulled forward. If the cut comes slightly LATE, the tension builds and the release is more powerful.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: Cut timing relative to expectation: early = propulsion, late = amplified release.
implications: Late cuts amplify the release felt at the cut

nodes.name: Movement Phrases — Build/Peak/Release
nodes.summary: Like music, editing has phrases — build to peak to release. Each phrase is a complete rhythmic unit.

details.principle: Like music, editing has phrases — build → peak → release. Each phrase is a complete rhythmic unit. Cutting mid-phrase (during the build, before the peak) feels premature. Cutting at the peak feels powerful. Cutting during the release feels comfortable and resolved.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: Identify phrase boundaries; cut at peak for power, at release for comfort.

nodes.name: Kinesthetic Empathy
nodes.summary: Viewers physically empathize with on-screen movement — the body mirrors the camera's movement through mirror neuron activation.

details.principle: Viewers physically empathize with on-screen movement. When the camera pushes in, the viewer's body feels forward motion. When speed ramps create deceleration, the viewer physically feels braking.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: zoom_push feels like 'leaning in'; zoom_pull_back feels like 'stepping away'. Speed ramps are felt as physical acceleration/deceleration.
implications: Camera movement is bodily experienced, not just observed
Mirror neuron activation underlies viewer engagement

nodes.name: The Pulse — On-Pulse vs Off-Pulse
nodes.summary: Underneath the surface rhythm of cuts, a sequence has an underlying pulse like a heartbeat. The art is in establishing a pulse and deviating from it at meaningful moments.

details.principle: Underneath the surface rhythm of cuts, a sequence has an underlying PULSE — like a heartbeat. Cuts can be ON the pulse (stability, satisfaction) or OFF the pulse (syncopation, tension, surprise). Being consistently on-pulse is metronomic and dead. Being consistently off-pulse is chaotic and anxious.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: Establish a pulse, then deviate from it strategically. All-on-pulse = dead. All-off-pulse = chaos. Variation = art.
implications: Pulse establishment then deviation drives engagement

nodes.name: Rhythmic Fractality
nodes.summary: The rhythms of a well-edited piece are fractal — shot-level rhythms echo scene-level rhythms echo overall structure rhythms.

details.principle: The rhythms of a well-edited piece are fractal. Shot-level rhythms echo scene-level rhythms echo overall structure rhythms. A scene that builds → peaks → releases mirrors the overall video's build → peak → resolution.
details.author: Karen Pearlman
details.application: Self-similarity at shot/scene/structure levels creates organic wholeness. Shot rhythms should mirror overall structure rhythm.
implications: Edit cohesion comes from rhythmic self-similarity at multiple scales
Each scene is a microcosm of the whole

nodes.name: Metric Montage
nodes.summary: Cuts at fixed time intervals regardless of content. Creates mechanical tension, escalation, inevitability — like a ticking clock.

details.principle: Cuts at fixed time intervals regardless of content. Creates mechanical tension, escalation, inevitability. Like a ticking clock. The interval can shorten progressively (acceleration) to build dread or excitement.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein, 'Film Form' (1949)
details.application: Used for: countdown sequences, time-pressure, rapid product showcases. In Editron: montage_mode with beat-locked cuts IS metric montage.

nodes.name: Rhythmic Montage
nodes.summary: Cuts based on the visual rhythm of the content. Action within the shots determines when to cut, not a fixed timer.

details.principle: Cuts based on the visual rhythm OF the content. The action within the shots determines when to cut — not a fixed timer. Creates organic flow, the video breathes with the action.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein
details.application: Used for: music-synced editing, dance, action sequences. In Editron: cut_on_action and high_motion_fast_pacing implement rhythmic montage principles.

nodes.name: Tonal Montage
nodes.summary: Cuts based on emotional tone — shots assembled by mood. Creates sustained emotional states, immersion.

details.principle: Cuts based on the emotional tone of shots, not their rhythm or timing. Shots are assembled by MOOD — dark shots grouped with dark shots, bright with bright. Creates sustained emotional states, immersion.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein
details.application: Used for: brand atmosphere pieces, emotional narratives, mood maintenance. In Editron: genre_parameters and moment_weight_map create the conditions for tonal montage.
implications: Genre and emotional weighting drive grouping

nodes.name: Overtonal Montage
nodes.summary: The combination of metric + rhythmic + tonal aligned simultaneously. The highest form of purely sensory montage.

details.principle: The combination of metric + rhythmic + tonal. All three dimensions aligned simultaneously. Creates complex, multilayered emotional experience. The highest form of purely sensory montage.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein
details.application: Used for: climactic sequences where everything converges. In Editron: cinematic_moment detection is essentially detecting overtonal convergence — multiple tracks peaking simultaneously.
examples: Cinematic moments where multiple tracks peak
implications: cinematic_moment detection is overtonal convergence detection
All three montage dimensions aligning simultaneously

nodes.name: Intellectual Montage
nodes.summary: Juxtaposition creates meaning neither shot has alone — 1+1=3. The viewer's brain creates the third meaning from the collision.

details.principle: The most radical — juxtaposition creates MEANING neither shot has alone. 1+1=3. A shot of a peacock followed by a shot of a politician = 'this politician is vain.' Neither shot says this alone. The viewer's brain creates the third meaning from the collision.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein
details.application: In Editron: match_cut is the closest technique. This level of meaning-making generally requires human creative direction — difficult to automate because the meaning is CONCEPTUAL, not signal-based.
implications: Meaning emerges from collision, not from individual shots
match_cut is the closest automated technique

nodes.name: Collision vs Linkage
nodes.summary: Eisenstein's collision (opposing elements juxtaposed for dialectical meaning) vs Pudovkin's linkage (smooth narrative connection). Most commercial editing is linkage.

details.principle: Eisenstein's approach (collision — opposing elements juxtaposed for dialectical meaning) contrasts with Pudovkin's approach (linkage — smooth connection between shots for narrative flow). Most commercial editing is linkage.
details.author: Sergei Eisenstein vs Vsevolod Pudovkin
details.application: Eisenstein's collision is used in: political content, artistic brand films, when the brand wants to make a POINT through visual argument. The smash_cut technique is the simplest form of collision.

nodes.name: Tarkovsky's Time-Pressure
nodes.summary: A shot contains time under pressure — the accumulation of information, emotion, and tension within the shot. Pressure comes from what the viewer KNOWS, not from what's ON SCREEN.

details.principle: A shot contains TIME under pressure. The 'pressure' is the accumulation of information, emotion, and tension within the shot. A boring shot has no time-pressure — nothing is accumulating. A charged shot has HIGH time-pressure even if 'nothing is happening.' The key insight: time-pressure comes from what the viewer KNOWS, not from what's ON SCREEN.
details.author: Andrei Tarkovsky, 'Sculpting in Time' (1986)
details.application: The narrative_pressure composite signal attempts to detect charged moments — but it can only approximate. True time-pressure requires understanding the STORY. The Unified Intelligence Engine's moment_weight_map identifies which moments carry narrative weight that signals alone can't detect.
examples: Empty chair where someone used to sit (charged)
Spinning top in Inception (high pressure from narrative context)
Long hallway with closed door at end (charged by accumulation)
Pause after 'We grew 300%' is charged; pause after 'So anyway...' is dead air
implications: Content determines pressure, not silence itself
narrative_pressure signal is only a proxy
moment weighting from LLM is the deeper authority
charged_silence_protection mapping uses narrative_pressure as proxy

nodes.name: Synchresis
nodes.summary: When sound and visual event occur simultaneously, the brain automatically fuses them into a single percept — even if the sound doesn't actually come from the visual source.

details.principle: When a sound and a visual event occur simultaneously, the brain automatically fuses them into a single percept — even if the sound doesn't actually come from the visual source. A random 'crack' at the moment someone sets down a cup = perceived as the cup's sound. The fusion is automatic and happens within ~40ms. Beyond 40ms offset, the brain separates them.
details.author: Michel Chion, 'Audio-Vision' (1994)
details.application: This is why SFX timing precision is non-negotiable — sfx_timing_drift < 3 frames constraint. SFX can be totally arbitrary as long as it lands on a visual event within the synchresis window.
examples: Random 'crack' at cup placement = perceived as cup sound
SFX synced within 40ms = fuses with visual
implications: Sound source need not be diegetic — only synced

nodes.name: The McGurk Effect
nodes.summary: Visual input changes what you hear. If you see a mouth saying 'ga' but hear 'ba,' the brain perceives 'da' — a fusion of both.

details.principle: Visual input changes what you HEAR. If you see a mouth saying 'ga' but hear 'ba,' the brain perceives 'da' — a fusion of both inputs. The visual mouth movement overrides the auditory signal.
details.author: McGurk & MacDonald (1976)
details.application: When a speaker's lip movements are visible, audio must be tightly synced. This is why cut_mid_word is a critical constraint — the viewer's brain is actively fusing mouth movement with speech sound.
implications: Lip-visible speakers require tight audio sync
Visual mouth movement overrides audio at perception level

nodes.name: Cross-Modal Correspondences
nodes.summary: The brain has innate mappings between senses: brightness ↔ pitch, size ↔ loudness, sharpness ↔ timbre. Audio and visual design should be coherent.

details.principle: The brain has innate mappings between senses: brightness ↔ pitch (bright images feel high-pitched), size ↔ loudness (large objects feel louder), sharpness ↔ timbre (angular shapes feel like sharp sounds, round shapes feel like smooth sounds). These correspondences mean that audio and visual design should be COHERENT.
details.author: Charles Spence (2011)
details.application: Bright visuals with high-pitched accents, dark visuals with low-frequency drones. Mismatches create subtle but real cognitive dissonance.
implications: Audio-visual design must be cross-modally coherent

nodes.name: Sound Symbolism (Bouba/Kiki)
nodes.summary: Round sounds ('bouba') feel soft, organic, friendly. Angular sounds ('kiki') feel sharp, precise, aggressive. This extends to editing transitions.

details.principle: Round sounds ('bouba') feel soft, organic, friendly. Angular sounds ('kiki') feel sharp, precise, aggressive. This extends to editing: round transitions (dissolve, blur) pair with soft sounds. Sharp transitions (hard cut, smash cut, flash) pair with impact sounds.
details.author: Sound symbolism research (bouba/kiki paradigm)
details.application: Round transitions (dissolve, blur) pair with soft sounds; sharp transitions (hard cut, smash cut, flash) pair with impact sounds. The viewer's brain expects this sensory coherence.
implications: Transition shape determines paired sound character

nodes.name: Frequency Masking
nodes.summary: When two sounds occupy the same frequency range, the louder masks the quieter. Speech (200Hz-4kHz) and music mid-range compete directly.

details.principle: When two sounds occupy the same frequency range, the louder one masks the quieter one. Speech (200Hz-4kHz) and music mid-range compete directly. This is why music ducking is a non-negotiable constraint — without it, the viewer can't hear the words. The solution: duck music mids specifically, not just overall level (the bass and highs can stay).
details.author: Psychoacoustics (frequency masking)
details.application: Duck music mids specifically (200Hz-4kHz range), not just overall level. Bass and highs can stay.
examples: Mid-frequency ducking preserves bass and highs
implications: Music ducking is non-negotiable when speech is present
Frequency-specific ducking is superior to broadband ducking

nodes.name: Predictive Processing in Film Viewing
nodes.summary: The brain is a prediction machine — constantly predicting next frame, next cut, next sound. Editing works by managing these predictions.

details.principle: The brain is a prediction machine. It constantly predicts the next frame, the next cut, the next sound. Editing works by MANAGING these predictions.
details.author: Karl Friston (predictive coding framework)
details.application: Frames editing as a system of confirmed and violated predictions. The signal system primarily produces CONFIRMED-prediction cuts. Deliberate prediction VIOLATIONS — the smash_cut, the syncopation, the held shot past expected cut point — are creative tools for surprise and emphasis.
implications: Both required: predictable baseline + strategic violations

nodes.name: Confirmed Predictions = Invisible Cuts
nodes.summary: When the brain correctly predicts the next shot (based on dialogue rhythm, visual cues, musical structure), the cut feels natural and invisible.

details.principle: When the brain correctly predicts the next shot (based on dialogue rhythm, visual cues, musical structure), the cut feels natural and invisible. This is Murch's 'invisible cut' — it works because the brain already expected it. Professional editors achieve this intuitively by cutting at 'blink points'.
details.author: Predictive processing / Murch synthesis
details.application: Signal-driven cuts at speech boundaries, beat positions, action peaks all confirm prediction.
implications: Beat positions, speech endings, action peaks are prediction-confirmed

nodes.name: Violated Predictions = Surprise/Tension/Engagement
nodes.summary: When the cut comes at an unexpected moment, the brain generates a prediction error. Theta oscillations spike at unpredicted edit boundaries.

details.principle: When the cut comes at an unexpected moment, or the incoming shot is unexpected, the brain generates a prediction error. Drew & Soto-Faraco (2024) showed that theta oscillations spike at unpredicted edit boundaries — the brain's 'wait, that wasn't expected' signal. This can be positive (delightful surprise, pattern interrupt, comedy) or negative (confusion, disorientation, annoyance). The difference depends on whether the violation SERVES the story.
details.author: Drew & Soto-Faraco (2024) — EEG + film editing
details.application: Strategic prediction violations at high-weight moments create engagement. Unmotivated violations create confusion.
examples: Held shots past expected cut create tension
implications: Theta oscillation spikes at unpredicted boundaries
Violations must serve the story to be positive

nodes.name: Event Segmentation Theory
nodes.summary: The brain segments continuous experience into discrete events at boundaries — moments where goals change, locations shift, or actors enter/exit. Cuts at boundaries are invisible.

details.principle: The brain naturally segments continuous experience into discrete events at 'event boundaries' — moments where goals change, locations shift, or actors enter/exit. Professional editors intuitively place cuts at these boundaries because that's where the brain EXPECTS a change. Cuts at event boundaries are invisible. Cuts within events are noticeable.
details.author: Zacks & Swallow (2007)
details.application: In Editron: topic_boundary signal detects semantic event boundaries. Cuts at these points feel natural. Cuts between them require stronger motivation (action, energy, rhythm).
implications: topic_boundary signal aligns with event segmentation
Boundary cuts are invisible by default

nodes.name: Attentional Synchrony in Film
nodes.summary: The mix of confirmed predictions (comfortable invisible cuts) and strategic violations (surprise, emphasis) is what keeps viewers engaged without exhausting them.

details.principle: The signal system primarily produces CONFIRMED-prediction cuts (rhythmically expected, at speech boundaries, at beat positions). Deliberate prediction VIOLATIONS — the smash_cut, the syncopation, the held shot past expected cut point — are the creative tools for surprise and emphasis. The system needs BOTH: a baseline of predictable cuts (comfortable, invisible) with strategic violations at high-weight moments (engaging, emphatic). A video that's all predictable is boring. A video that's all surprising is exhausting.
details.author: Synthesis of predictive coding + editing practice
details.application: Both predictable baseline and strategic violations are required. All-predictable = boring. All-surprising = exhausting.

nodes.name: Kishōtenketsu (起承転結) — East Asian Four-Act Structure
nodes.summary: Introduction → Development → Twist → Reconciliation. Builds without conflict — no antagonist, no problem to solve. The 'twist' is a perspective shift, not a confrontation.

details.principle: Introduction (起) → Development (承) → Twist (転) → Reconciliation (結). Crucially, it builds WITHOUT CONFLICT. There is no antagonist, no problem to solve. The 'twist' is a perspective shift, not a confrontation. The resolution is HARMONY, not victory.
details.author: Classical East Asian narrative tradition
details.application: For brands that don't want to frame value as 'solving a problem' — comfort/lifestyle, food, family, cultural celebration — Kishōtenketsu is more authentic than three-act problem/solution.
details.culturalContext: East Asian (Japanese, Chinese, Korean). Native to Japanese manga, Chinese classical poetry, Korean drama.

nodes.name: Rasa Theory — Indian Classical Aesthetics
nodes.summary: Nine aesthetic emotions (rasas). Content organized around evoking a specific rasa rather than following a plot structure. Predates Western narrative theory by over a millennium.

details.principle: Nine aesthetic emotions (rasas): Shringara (love/beauty), Hasya (humor), Karuna (compassion/sorrow), Raudra (fury), Veera (heroism), Bhayanaka (terror), Bibhatsa (disgust), Adbhuta (wonder), Shanta (peace). Content can be organized around evoking a specific rasa rather than following a plot structure.
details.author: Bharata's Natyashastra (~200 BCE)
details.application: A food ad might target Shringara + Adbhuta. A sports ad might target Veera + Raudra. This predates Western narrative theory by over a millennium and offers a fundamentally different way to think about 'what should this content make the viewer feel?'
details.culturalContext: Indian classical aesthetics. Foundational text: Bharata's Natyashastra (~200 BCE). Predates Western narrative theory.

nodes.name: Bollywood Visual Grammar
nodes.summary: Center framing for protagonists, crash zooms for emphasis, orbit shots for hero introductions. Dynamic camera as emotional participant. Rich saturation.

details.principle: Center framing for protagonists (hero gets frame center — power position). Crash zooms for dramatic emphasis (reaction shots, villain reveals). Orbit shots for hero introductions (camera circles the protagonist in glory). Song sequences have their own visual language: wide for choreography, close-up for lip-sync, rapid intercutting for energy. Dynamic camera as emotional participant, not passive observer. Rich saturation — gold, magenta, deep red, emerald. Color IS expression. High edit density during musical sequences (16-24 cuts/min), deliberate pacing for contrast during dialogue.
details.author: Indian commercial cinema tradition
details.application: Center frame = protagonist; crash zoom = dramatic emphasis; orbit = hero introduction; song sequences use wide/CU/intercut grammar.
examples: Color palette: gold, magenta, deep red, emerald
implications: Camera is emotional participant, not observer
Color is expression, not just palette

nodes.name: K-Drama Editing Patience
nodes.summary: Shots hold 30-100% longer than Western equivalents. The 'reaction hold' — 3-5 seconds of sustained close-up on a face — is signature.

details.principle: Shots hold 30-100% LONGER than Western equivalents. The 'reaction hold' — 3-5 seconds of sustained close-up on a face after dialogue, in silence — is a signature technique. The viewer reads the face. The silence IS the content. Soft focus, shallow DOF for intimacy. Naturalistic framing. The camera OBSERVES with patience — it lets moments breathe. Golden hour lighting for romance is practically mandatory.
details.author: Korean drama tradition
details.application: Hold durations 30-100% longer than Western default. Reaction holds 3-5s. Silence is content. Soft focus + shallow DOF + naturalistic framing.
details.culturalContext: Korean (K-Drama) tradition. Counter to fast-cut Western/algorithmic content.

nodes.name: Nordic/Scandinavian Minimalism
nodes.summary: Static wide shots with negative space. Muted compositions. The landscape IS a character. Stillness as a storytelling tool.

details.principle: Static wide shots with negative space. Muted compositions. Minimal camera movement. Deep focus. Desaturated, low-contrast, cool-dominant color. Gray and blue-green palette. Stillness as a storytelling tool. The landscape IS a character. Silence is comfortable, not empty. This aesthetic values what's NOT there as much as what is. Editing interventions (zooms, graphics, SFX) should be minimal — the content speaks through restraint.
details.author: Nordic/Scandinavian cinematic tradition
details.application: Static wides + negative space + deep focus + desaturated cool palette. Landscape as character. Restraint over intervention.

nodes.name: Latin American Visual Energy
nodes.summary: Warm, saturated compositions. Close physical proximity. Handheld energy. Telenovela tradition: dramatic close-ups, emotional eye lines.

details.principle: Warm, saturated compositions. Close physical proximity between subjects. Handheld energy. Fluid tracking shots through tight spaces. Telenovela tradition: dramatic close-ups, emotional eye lines, heightened composition. Color is warm, contrast is high, earth tones dominate. The editing rhythm follows emotional escalation (tonal montage), not strict timing.
details.author: Latin American cinema and television tradition
details.application: Warm saturated palette + handheld + close subject proximity + tonal-montage emotional escalation.
details.culturalContext: Latin American cinema and television, especially the telenovela tradition.

nodes.name: Middle Eastern/Arab Cinema
nodes.summary: Geometric framing influenced by Islamic architectural patterns. Symmetry as visual principle. Warm desert palettes. Long takes that respect the weight of moments.

details.principle: Geometric framing influenced by Islamic architectural patterns. Symmetry as visual principle. Warm desert palettes — gold, deep blue, turquoise accents. Deliberate pacing. Long takes that respect the weight of moments. Contemporary Gulf content increasingly blends this with high-production Western technique.
details.author: Middle Eastern/Arab cinematic tradition
details.application: Geometric/symmetric framing + warm desert palette (gold, deep blue, turquoise) + long takes + deliberate pacing.
details.culturalContext: Middle Eastern/Arab cinema. Influenced by Islamic architectural patterns. Contemporary Gulf content blends with Western technique.

nodes.name: Japanese Live-Action
nodes.summary: Ozu's tatami-level camera (low, static, observational) remains influential. Stillness and composition privileged over movement. Wide range in pacing — sub-1s for action, 5-10s for emotion.

details.principle: Ozu's tatami-level camera (low, static, observational) remains influential. Stillness and composition privileged over movement. Wide range in pacing — anime uses sub-1s cuts for action and 5-10+ second holds for emotion. The common thread is intentionality — every shot earns its duration, whether that's 0.5s or 15s.
details.author: Japanese cinematic tradition (Yasujirō Ozu lineage)
details.application: Tatami-level (low static observational) camera + stillness/composition primacy + bimodal pacing (very fast for action, very slow for emotion).
details.culturalContext: Japanese live-action and animation cinema. Foundational influence: Yasujirō Ozu.

nodes.name: Nollywood (Nigerian)
nodes.summary: Direct framing, conversational medium shots, practical locations, mobile-first composition awareness, strong close-ups for dialogue-heavy storytelling.

details.principle: Direct framing, conversational medium shots, practical locations, mobile-first composition awareness, strong close-ups for dialogue-heavy storytelling. Growing cinematographic sophistication while maintaining accessibility and directness.
details.author: Nigerian (Nollywood) cinematic tradition
details.application: Conversational medium shots + practical locations + mobile-first composition + dialogue close-ups.
details.culturalContext: Nigerian (Nollywood) cinema, the second-largest film industry by output.

nodes.name: Vonnegut's Story Shapes
nodes.summary: Every story is a curve on a good-fortune axis. 'Man in Hole' (things get worse, then better) is the most universal. The shape determines where the viewer's emotions go.

details.principle: Every story is a curve on a good-fortune axis. 'Man in Hole' (things get worse, then get better) is the most universal. The shape determines where the viewer's emotions go.
details.author: Kurt Vonnegut
details.application: Every narrative structure can be described as a curve on a good-fortune/tension axis. Use the curve shape to plan emotional progression.
examples: Man in Hole = down then up
Boy Meets Girl = up, down, up
implications: Plot is secondary to emotional curve
Map every structure to a fortune curve

nodes.name: McKee's Gap Theory
nodes.summary: Story = gap between expectation and result. Every scene starts with a character expecting something. What actually happens is different. That gap IS the story.

details.principle: Story = gap between expectation and result. Every scene starts with a character expecting something. What actually happens is different. That gap IS the story. If no gap exists (everything goes as expected), there's no story — just information.
details.author: Robert McKee
details.application: Every scene must contain a gap. No gap = pure information delivery, not story. Editor must locate and emphasize gaps.
examples: Character expects A, B happens = story
Character expects A, A happens = information
implications: Gap is the elemental unit of story
Information without gap is not story
Each scene must produce expectation-result mismatch

nodes.name: The Zeigarnik Effect
nodes.summary: Unresolved questions create cognitive tension that drives retention. Open loops (questions asked but not yet answered) keep viewers watching.

details.principle: Unresolved questions create cognitive tension that drives retention. Open loops (questions asked but not yet answered) keep viewers watching. Every structure uses this — the question 'what happens next?' is the retention engine.
details.author: Bluma Zeigarnik
details.application: Use open loops to drive retention. Question 'what happens next?' is the universal retention engine across all structures.
implications: Resolved questions release tension; keep them open
All narrative structures depend on Zeigarnik tension

nodes.name: Three-Act Structure
nodes.summary: Setup → Confrontation → Resolution. Stability → Disruption → New stability. Universal but Western-dominant.

details.principle: Shape: Setup → Confrontation → Resolution. Emotional arc: Stability → Disruption → New stability.
details.author: Western dramatic tradition (Aristotle lineage)
details.application: Best for: product ads with problem/solution, brand narratives, explainers. Compression to 30-60s: hook (0-5s) = setup, body (5-40s) = confrontation, close (40-60s) = resolution.
implications: 'Problem' framing can feel aggressive in harmony-oriented cultures
details.culturalContext: Universal but Western-dominant. 'Problem' framing can feel aggressive in harmony-oriented cultures.

nodes.name: Five-Act Structure (Freytag's Pyramid)
nodes.summary: Exposition → Rising Action → Climax → Falling Action → Denouement. For longer-form content.

details.principle: Shape: Exposition → Rising Action → Climax → Falling Action → Denouement.
details.author: Gustav Freytag (Freytag's Pyramid)
details.application: Best for: longer content (2-5 min), brand films, documentary-style. Compression: rarely works below 60s — too many beats.
implications: Five distinct beats need time to land

nodes.name: Hero's Journey / Monomyth
nodes.summary: Ordinary World → Call → Threshold → Ordeal → Reward → Return. Deeply Western. Resonates most with individualist cultures.

details.principle: Shape: Ordinary World → Call → Threshold → Ordeal → Reward → Return.
details.author: Joseph Campbell / Christopher Vogler
details.application: Best for: testimonials, founder stories, transformation narratives, fitness/health.
implications: Transformation is the heart of the structure
details.culturalContext: Deeply Western. Resonates most with individualist cultures.

nodes.name: Dan Harmon's Story Circle (8 beats)
nodes.summary: Comfort → Want → Unfamiliar → Adapt → Find → Pay → Return → Change. Designed for episodic TV — each piece complete but connected.

details.principle: Shape: Comfort → Want → Unfamiliar → Adapt → Find → Pay → Return → Change.
details.author: Dan Harmon
details.application: Best for: episodic content, series, recurring campaigns. Designed for episodic TV — each piece complete but connected.

nodes.name: Kishōtenketsu (起承転結) — Narrative Structure
nodes.summary: Introduction → Development → Twist → Reconciliation. Builds without conflict — increasingly relevant globally.

details.principle: Shape: Introduction → Development → Twist → Reconciliation.
details.author: Classical East Asian narrative tradition
details.application: Best for: lifestyle brands, food/beverage, family, cultural celebration. Native East Asian. Builds without conflict. Increasingly relevant globally.
details.culturalContext: Native East Asian (Japanese, Chinese, Korean). Increasingly relevant globally.

nodes.name: Save the Cat (Blake Snyder, 15 beats)
nodes.summary: 15-beat detailed structure for long-form brand films, short films, narrative cinema ads. Too many beats for sub-2-minute content.

details.principle: 15-beat narrative structure derived from screenwriting analysis.
details.author: Blake Snyder
details.application: Best for: long-form brand films (3-10 min), short films, narrative cinema ads. Too many beats for anything under 2 minutes.

nodes.name: Pixar Story Spine
nodes.summary: 'Once upon a time... Every day... Until one day... Because of that... Until finally... And ever since then...' Forces causal connection between events.

details.principle: Shape: 'Once upon a time... Every day... Until one day... Because of that... Until finally... And ever since then...'
details.author: Pixar / Kenn Adams
details.application: Best for: founder stories, product origin, change narratives. Forces CAUSAL connection between events — 'because of that' prevents random sequences. Excellent LLM prompt structure.

nodes.name: Rasa-Based Design (Indian Classical)
nodes.summary: Not linear — organized by evoking a specific aesthetic emotion (rasa). For content using Indian aesthetic tradition.

details.principle: Shape: not linear — organized by evoking a specific aesthetic emotion (rasa).
details.author: Bharata's Natyashastra / Indian classical aesthetics
details.application: Best for: content designed for Indian audiences or using Indian aesthetic tradition. Application: food ad → Shringara (beauty) + Adbhuta (wonder). Sports → Veera (heroism) + Raudra (fury).
details.culturalContext: Indian classical aesthetics. Best for Indian audiences or content using Indian aesthetic tradition.

nodes.name: Hook-Value-CTA
nodes.summary: Attention grab → Deliver value → Ask for action. The default short-form structure when no other fits.

details.principle: Shape: Attention grab → Deliver value → Ask for action.
details.author: Social media / direct response convention
details.application: Best for: social media ads, product demos, educational, most sub-60s commercial. Default: when no other structure fits, this works.

nodes.name: Problem-Agitate-Solve (PAS)
nodes.summary: Name the pain → Make it worse → Offer solution. Direct response standard. Can feel manipulative in cultures valuing subtlety.

details.principle: Shape: Name the pain → Make it worse → Offer solution.
details.author: Direct response copywriting tradition
details.application: Best for: direct response, SaaS demos, health/wellness, clear pain points. Can feel manipulative in cultures valuing subtlety. Use gently in East Asian and Nordic markets.
details.culturalContext: Western direct response tradition. Can feel manipulative in cultures valuing subtlety. Use gently in East Asian and Nordic markets.

nodes.name: Before/After Transformation
nodes.summary: 'Before' state → Transformation moment → 'After' state. The cut between before and after is the most important cut.

details.principle: Shape: 'Before' state → Transformation moment → 'After' state.
details.author: Transformation marketing convention
details.application: Best for: fitness, beauty, renovation, cleaning, any visual transformation. Key: the cut between before and after is the most important cut. Use strongest transition — match cut, whip pan, or flash. Dissolve undermines impact.
implications: Strongest transitions: match cut, whip pan, flash

nodes.name: Myth-Truth (Pattern Interrupt)
nodes.summary: State common belief → Shatter it → Replace with truth. Educational, contrarian positioning, 'everything you know is wrong' hooks.

details.principle: Shape: State common belief → Shatter it → Replace with truth.
details.author: Educational/contrarian content convention
details.application: Best for: educational, contrarian positioning, 'everything you know is wrong' hooks. Key: the 'shatter' moment needs audio support — record scratch, impact hit, or silence. Visual: zoom punch or flash.
implications: Shatter moment requires audio support: record scratch, impact, or silence

nodes.name: Countdown/Ranking
nodes.summary: #N → #N-1 → ... → #1. Inherently retention-boosting — viewer wants to see #1.

details.author: List-content convention
details.application: Best for: listicles, comparisons, 'top X' content. Why: inherently retention-boosting — viewer wants to see #1. Each item is a micro-resolution that re-hooks.

nodes.name: Day-in-the-Life
nodes.summary: Morning → Activities → Evening. Strong in Japanese (密着) and Korean vlog cultures.

details.principle: Shape: Morning → Activities → Evening.
details.author: Vlog/lifestyle content convention
details.application: Best for: influencer/creator, behind-the-scenes, company culture, vlog-style.
details.culturalContext: Especially popular in Japanese content culture (密着 — 'attached observation'). Strong in Korean vlog culture.

nodes.name: Testimonial Arc
nodes.summary: Who I am → My problem → How I found solution → My result → My recommendation.

details.principle: Shape: Who I am → My problem → How I found solution → My result → My recommendation.
details.author: Testimonial/customer story convention
details.application: Best for: customer stories, reviews, case studies.

nodes.name: Versus/Comparison
nodes.summary: Option A → Option B → (Verdict). Visual: split-screen or alternating shots with consistent framing.

details.principle: Shape: Option A → Option B → (Verdict).
details.author: Comparison-content convention
details.application: Best for: product comparisons, 'this vs that,' competitive positioning. Visual: split-screen or alternating shots with consistent framing.

nodes.name: Challenge/Attempt
nodes.summary: Set challenge → Attempt(s) → Outcome. For social challenges, product stress tests, 'will it work?' content.

details.principle: Shape: Set challenge → Attempt(s) → Outcome.
details.author: Challenge-content convention
details.application: Best for: social challenges, product stress tests, 'will it work?'

nodes.name: Loop/Infinite Scroll
nodes.summary: End leads seamlessly back to beginning. Last frame matches first frame composition. Audio loops seamlessly.

details.principle: Shape: end leads seamlessly back to beginning.
details.author: Algorithmic short-form convention
details.application: Best for: short-form optimized for replay (algorithm rewards replays). Key: last frame matches first frame composition. Audio loops seamlessly.

nodes.name: The Reveal/Unboxing
nodes.summary: Concealment → Build anticipation → Reveal → Reaction. Product launches, mystery/surprise.

details.principle: Shape: Concealment → Build anticipation → Reveal → Reaction.
details.author: Reveal-content convention
details.application: Best for: product launches, unboxing, mystery/surprise content.

nodes.name: Micro-Narrative Stack
nodes.summary: Story 1 (3-5s) → Story 2 (3-5s) → Story 3 → ... → Theme emerges. Hard cuts between stories. Consistent music as connecting thread.

details.principle: Shape: Story 1 (3-5s) → Story 2 (3-5s) → Story 3 → ... → Theme emerges.
details.author: Multi-vignette content convention
details.application: Best for: testimonial compilations, multi-use-case ads, community content. Key: hard cuts between stories. Consistent music as connecting thread.

nodes.name: In Medias Res
nodes.summary: Start at climax → Flash back → Catch up → Continue. Color/filter shift between timelines.

details.principle: Shape: Start at climax → Flash back → Catch up → Continue.
details.author: Classical non-linear narrative tradition (Aristotle/Homer lineage)
details.application: Best for: high-stakes, dramatic, event recaps. Key: opening shot must be visually striking enough to earn the non-linear approach. Color/filter shift between timelines (desaturated flashback, full color present).
implications: Opening shot must be visually striking
Color/filter signal time shifts (desaturated past, full present)

nodes.name: Circular Narrative
nodes.summary: Starts and ends with same image/moment, but with changed meaning. Bookend shots composed identically with subtle differences.

details.principle: Shape: Starts and ends with same image/moment, but with changed meaning.
details.author: Literary circular structure tradition
details.application: Best for: brand films, emotional storytelling, 'full circle' campaigns. Key: bookend shots should be composed identically but with subtle differences.

nodes.name: Fragmented/Mosaic
nodes.summary: Disconnected pieces assembling into meaning — viewer constructs the story. For art-house, music videos, mood pieces.

details.principle: Shape: Disconnected pieces assembling into meaning — viewer constructs the story.
details.author: Experimental/art-film tradition
details.application: Best for: art-house brand films, music videos, experimental, mood pieces. Risk: requires viewer trust. Works for premium positioning, risky for mass commercial.
implications: Risky for mass commercial — requires trust

nodes.name: Parallel Narrative (Cross-Cutting)
nodes.summary: Two or more stories told simultaneously, converging at the end. 'Two worlds collide,' simultaneous timelines.

details.principle: Shape: Two or more stories told simultaneously, converging at the end.
details.author: Cross-cutting narrative tradition (Griffith lineage)
details.application: Best for: 'two worlds collide,' product connecting different users, simultaneous timelines.

nodes.name: Structure Selection Guide
nodes.summary: Select narrative structure by content type, duration, brand voice, cultural context, platform, and emotional goal. Work backwards from target emotion.

details.principle: The LLM Scene Parser should select based on: 1) Content type — what is being communicated? 2) Duration — structures with many beats need more time. 3) Brand voice — confrontational brands → PAS, Myth-Truth. Warm brands → Kishōtenketsu, Day-in-the-Life. 4) Cultural context — target audience's storytelling traditions. 5) Platform — TikTok rewards hooks and loops. YouTube allows slower builds. LinkedIn rewards educational framing. 6) Emotional goal — what should the viewer FEEL at the end? Work backwards from target emotion.
details.author: Editron synthesis
details.application: LLM Scene Parser uses these 6 axes to select narrative structure for any project.

nodes.name: The Automatic Car Principle
nodes.summary: UX philosophy governing all creative decisions: auto mode = professional output by default, manual mode always available, heavy lifting never leaves the system.

details.principle: Auto mode (default): User provides input → professional output. Platform makes all editorial decisions automatically. Every decision is deterministic and rule-driven. User doesn't need to understand the decisions. Manual mode (always available): User can override ANY decision at ANY point. Switching is instant and lossless — no regeneration. Heavy lifting never leaves: Even in full manual mode, the system handles color grading (skin-tone protection), audio mixing (LUFS, ducking), asset management (CDN, versioning), quality review (anti-pattern detection), render pipeline.
details.author: Insturix Vision
details.application: Constraint on constraints — governs how Parts 1-4 are applied, not what they contain. The LLM uses all theory in Part 5 internally; the user should never need to know this theory exists. The theory produces the result; the result is what the user experiences.
examples: System uses Pearlman's breath model internally; user sees 'pacing feels natural'
System uses Murch's Rule of Six internally; user sees 'cuts feel right'
implications: Auto mode produces professional output by default
Manual override always available, instant, lossless
Heavy lifting (LUFS, codecs, color) always handled even in manual
Theory is internal; result is what the user experiences
